summary.text: Daughter of Ligdus and Telethusa near Phaestus, raised as a boy because her father vowed to expose any girl-child — who loved the maiden Ianthe and, on the eve of their wedding, was changed into a man by Isis at her mother's prayer.

story.text: Near Phaestus and Gnossus lived Ligdus, poor but honest, and his wife Telethusa. When she was with child he swore to kill the infant if it were a girl, for they could not afford a dowry. Isis appeared to Telethusa in a dream and forbade the exposure; when a daughter was born the mother lied and named her Iphis after the grandfather.

Iphis grew up with a girl's face but a boy's dress, and no one suspected the fraud except the nurse. When the time came to marry, Ligdus betrothed Iphis to Ianthe, fairest of the Cretan girls — and Iphis loved her with a love that seemed impossible, for both seemed maidens to the world.

On the eve of the wedding Telethusa and Iphis prayed in Isis' temple. The goddess nodded; when mother and daughter left, Iphis walked with a lengthened stride, darker face, and short hair — a man in form. Venus and Hymenaeus came to the marriage fire, and Iphis took Ianthe as his bride.

The atlas keeps this Cretan Iphis distinct from `iphis-anaxagoras`, king in the native third of Argos, and from the inset Iphis of Salamis in Pomona's orchard tale — a youth who hanged himself for scorned love, not the bride changed by Isis.
